entries.meaning: To head straight toward something, or to be the thing that produces a certain result.
examples: As soon as the credits rolled she made for the exit.
The dog made straight for the water.
We made for higher ground as soon as the river came up.
Two connecting flights make for a very long day.
Rain in the fourth quarter made for a sloppy game.
Cheap parts make for expensive repairs later.

senses.head: Head toward, move in the direction of
body: Physical movement with a destination in mind, and usually in a hurry — you make for an exit, a door, higher ground. (направляться к, устремляться к)
examples: As soon as the credits rolled she made for the exit.
The dog made straight for the water.
We made for higher ground as soon as the river came up.

senses.head: Produce a result, contribute to
body: The subject is a situation rather than a person, and what follows is the outcome: makes for a long day, makes for good television. (способствовать, приводить к, обеспечивать)
examples: Two connecting flights make for a very long day.
Rain in the fourth quarter made for a sloppy game.
Cheap parts make for expensive repairs later.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays back on the verb and for is reduced to /fɚ/
entries.separable: no — for never lets go of its object. ✗ made the door for, and with a pronoun the object still follows the whole phrase: made for it, never ✗ made it for.
entries.transitive: yes, there is always something after for
entries.verb type: both — action in sense 1, dynamic physical movement toward a goal (she made for the exit). Sense 2 is stative, a situation standing in a relation to its result, and it resists the progressive: ✗ rain is making for a sloppy game.
entries.passive: no — the prepositional passive fails in both senses: ✗ the exit was made for, ✗ a long day is made for by two connecting flights.
entries.see also: make off, run for

entries.meaning: To form an opinion about something, or to treat it as significant.
examples: What do you make of the new manager?
I didn't know what to make of her answer.
Nobody could make much of the handwriting on the envelope.
The jury will make what it likes of his silence.
"You're late." "You want to make something of it?"
The papers made a great deal of one careless sentence.
He never made anything of the fact that he had paid for it himself.

senses.head: Interpret, form an opinion
body: Nearly always a question or a negative — what do you make of…, I don't know what to make of… You cannot use it to report an opinion you already hold. (понимать, думать о, истолковывать)
examples: What do you make of the new manager?
I didn't know what to make of her answer.
Nobody could make much of the handwriting on the envelope.
The jury will make what it likes of his silence.

senses.head: Make something of it — treat as an issue
body: Confrontational in the first shape (want to make something of it?) and simply "give weight to" in make much of. (раздувать, придавать значение; «имеешь что-то против?»)
examples: "You're late." "You want to make something of it?"
The papers made a great deal of one careless sentence.
He never made anything of the fact that he had paid for it himself.

entries.pronunciation note: stress on the verb; of is unstressed and said /əv/
entries.type: prepositional verb, in the frame make something of something
entries.separable: no — of stays glued to its object, but the frame always puts a word in front of it: make nothing of it, what do you make of her? ✗ make of it nothing.
entries.transitive: yes, and doubly so — it needs both an object and an of phrase
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, the act of forming or voicing an opinion. No stative or linking use; the frame needs both a what / much / nothing object and an of phrase.
entries.passive: restricted — natural only in sense 2, where the quantity is promoted: a great deal was made of one careless sentence. Sense 1 has no passive at all: ✗ what is made of the new manager?
entries.see also: make out, read into

entries.meaning: To leave in a hurry, especially in order to escape.
examples: The two of them made off before anyone thought to call the police.
He made off down the alley with the alarm still ringing.
The raccoons make off the second the porch light comes on.
Whoever hit the mailbox had made off by the time we got outside.
She made off in the middle of the ceremony and nobody noticed until dessert.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the verb takes no object, so no word can come between make and off.
entries.transitive: no, never takes an object; for the thing carried away use make off with
entries.register: everyday — very common in news writing about crime
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of hurried escape, always with a human or animal subject. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so there is nothing to promote: ✗ was made off, ✗ the alley was made off down.
entries.see also: make off with, run away, run off

entries.meaning: To steal something and get away with it.
examples: Someone made off with my bike right off the porch.
Two men made off with the register and a box of receipts.
The gulls made off with half of my sandwich.
He left the laptop on the seat and a kid made off with it.
A former partner had made off with most of the deposits before the audit.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase, pronoun or not. ✗ made the bike off with, ✗ made it off with; it is made off with it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive: taking something and fleeing with it. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part passive is marginal in American English: ?my bike was made off with, ✗ it was made off with by a kid. Say was stolen instead.
entries.see also: make off, run off with, run away with

entries.meaning: To manage to see, hear, or understand something; and, in other senses, to fare, to write out, to claim, or to kiss.
examples: I could just make out a figure at the end of the dock.
The signature was so faded that I couldn't make it out.
Read the sign and tell me whether you can make the street name out.
How did you make out at the DMV?
Their first store made out better than anyone expected.
Make the check out to the county clerk.
She made the receipt out for the full amount.
He makes himself out to be some kind of expert.
The article made out that the whole delay was the mayor's fault.
They were making out in the back row of the theater.
She admitted she had made out with him at the party.

senses.head: Discern, manage to see or hear
body: Almost always with can/could, and very often negative — the thing is at the edge of what your eyes or ears can handle. (разобрать, различить, расслышать)
examples: I could just make out a figure at the end of the dock.
The signature was so faded that I couldn't make it out.
Read the sign and tell me whether you can make the street name out.

senses.head: Manage, fare, get on
body: Intransitive and thoroughly American, usually in a question about how something went. (справляться, преуспевать)
examples: How did you make out at the DMV?
Their first store made out better than anyone expected.

senses.head: Write out a check or a form
body: The money sense; the payee follows to. (выписывать (чек, документ))
examples: Make the check out to the county clerk.
She made the receipt out for the full amount.

senses.head: Claim, represent as
body: With that or with out to be, and always with a hint that the claim is false. (изображать, выставлять (кем-л.))
examples: He makes himself out to be some kind of expert.
The article made out that the whole delay was the mayor's fault.

senses.head: Kiss and grope
body: Informal American, intransitive, often make out with someone. Not used in careful writing. (целоваться, обжиматься)
examples: They were making out in the back row of the theater.
She admitted she had made out with him at the party.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — make it OUT, not MAKE it out
entries.separable: yes — make out the address or make the address out, and with a pronoun the object must split the pair: make it out, never ✗ make out it. Senses 2 and 5 take no object at all, so nothing separates there.
entries.register: everyday; the kissing sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 2–5 (faring, writing out a check, claiming, kissing). Sense 1 is a perception verb close to stative: it lives with can / could and avoids the progressive, ✗ I am making out a figure.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the signature could barely be made out, the check was made out to the county clerk, he was made out to be some kind of expert. Intransitive senses 2 and 5 have none: ✗ was made out at the DMV.
entries.see also: make of, make up, read off, put together

entries.meaning: To change how something looks from top to bottom, or to sign property over to somebody.
examples: They made over the basement into a rec room.
We made the whole front porch over in one weekend.
The agency made him over before the first debate.
She made over the deed to her daughter in 1998.
The farm had been made over to a trust years before he died.
He made the whole account over to his brother and moved to Tucson.

senses.head: Transform, redo completely
body: Rooms, wardrobes, images, brands. The noun makeover is heard more often than the verb. (переделать, преобразить, переоборудовать)
examples: They made over the basement into a rec room.
We made the whole front porch over in one weekend.
The agency made him over before the first debate.

senses.head: Transfer ownership to
body: Legal and formal, always with to. (переписать, передать (имущество))
examples: She made over the deed to her daughter in 1998.
The farm had been made over to a trust years before he died.
He made the whole account over to his brother and moved to Tucson.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a makeover moves it to the front, MAKE-oh-ver
entries.separable: yes — make over the basement or make the basement over, and a pronoun must go in the middle: make it over, never ✗ make over it.
entries.register: everyday; the property sense is formal and legal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, the physical transformation and the legal transfer of property. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, and common in both — the basement was made over into a rec room; the farm had been made over to a trust years before he died.
entries.see also: make up, put up

entries.meaning: To invent something, to form a whole, to settle a quarrel, or to make good on what was missed.
examples: He made up a story about a flat tire.
She made the whole thing up on the drive over.
Don't make it up — just say you forgot.
Volunteers make up almost half of the staff.
Six counties make up the district.
They fought all week and made up on Sunday.
She has never made up with her sister.
I'll make up the hours on Saturday.
He made the missed quiz up after school.
The runner made it up on the last lap.
She was made up for the stage lights, not for daylight.
The pharmacy made up the prescription in ten minutes.
Could you make the guest bed up before they get here?

senses.head: Invent, fabricate
body: Stories, excuses, names, rules. The implication is that none of it is true. (выдумывать, сочинять, придумывать)
examples: He made up a story about a flat tire.
She made the whole thing up on the drive over.
Don't make it up — just say you forgot.

senses.head: Constitute, form
body: Statistical and structural: the parts are the subject and the whole follows. This sense never separates. (составлять, образовывать)
examples: Volunteers make up almost half of the staff.
Six counties make up the district.

senses.head: Reconcile after a quarrel
body: Intransitive, often make up with someone. (мириться, помириться)
examples: They fought all week and made up on Sunday.
She has never made up with her sister.

senses.head: Make good on what was missed
body: Hours, work, a test, lost ground. (навёрстывать, отрабатывать, восполнять)
examples: I'll make up the hours on Saturday.
He made the missed quiz up after school.
The runner made it up on the last lap.

senses.head: Apply cosmetics
body: Usually reflexive or passive — made up, make yourself up. (краситься, гримировать)
examples: She was made up for the stage lights, not for daylight.

senses.head: Prepare, put together
body: Beds, prescriptions, lists, packages. (готовить, составлять, приготовлять)
examples: The pharmacy made up the prescription in ten minutes.
Could you make the guest bed up before they get here?

entries.pronunciation note: the particle takes the stress — make it UP; the noun makeup is stressed on the front, MAKE-up
entries.separable: yes in most senses — make up a story or make the story up, and a pronoun must separate them: make it up, never ✗ make up it. Two exceptions worth memorizing: the "constitute" sense never separates (women make up half the class, ✗ make half the class up), and the "reconcile" sense has no object at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 3–6 (inventing, reconciling, catching up, applying cosmetics, preparing). Sense 2, 'constitute', is stative and refuses the progressive: ✗ volunteers are making up half the staff.
entries.passive: restricted — fine in the dynamic senses: the story was made up on the drive over, the prescription was made up in ten minutes, she was made up for the stage lights. Sense 2 passivizes only in the fixed be made up of — the district is made up of six counties, never ✗ made up by six counties — and sense 3 is intransitive: ✗ she was made up with.
entries.see also: make up for, make out, make over, put together

entries.meaning: To offset something bad or missing with something good.
examples: The view makes up for the stairs.
No bonus is going to make up for three lost weekends.
She worked doubles all month to make up for the time off.
Nothing makes up for it, but the apology helped.
Good coffee made up for a thin breakfast.
He has been trying to make up for that one remark ever since.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase. ✗ make lost time up for, ✗ make it up for; it is make up for it. Do not confuse it with the four-word make it up to someone, where it really does sit in the middle: I'll make it up to you.
entries.verb type: both — action when a person compensates (she worked doubles to make up for the time off), stative when a thing simply offsets another, where the progressive is odd: the view makes up for the stairs, ✗ the view is making up for the stairs.
entries.passive: restricted — stiff at best, and only with the loss as subject: ?the lost time will be made up for. ✗ the stairs are made up for by the view.
entries.see also: make up, pay back, pay off

entries.meaning: To flatter somebody in order to get something out of them.
examples: He spent the whole term making up to the department head.
She was making up to the neighbors long before she asked about the fence.
You can tell he wants something by the way he makes up to her.
Nobody who made up to the old man was in the will.
Stop making up to me and just ask.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the person follows the whole phrase: making up to the boss, making up to him. ✗ make the boss up to.
entries.transitive: yes, and the object is always a person
entries.register: British — an American would say suck up to or butter up. Note that American make it up to someone looks similar but means to compensate them, which is a different verb entirely.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive, flattering somebody for gain; the object is always a person. British, where American English says suck up to or butter up.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the department head was made up to, ✗ she was made up to by the neighbors. The prepositional passive is simply unavailable here.
entries.see also: make up for, pay off

entries.meaning: To get together with somebody by arrangement, usually informally.
examples: Let's meet up after work.
We met up at the taco place on Third.
The two groups meet up every spring in Denver.
They had already met up by the time I got the text.
If the flight lands early we can meet up before the game.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a meetup moves it forward, MEET-up
entries.separable: nothing to separate — no object follows, so nothing can sit between meet and up. For the person you are meeting, use meet up with.
entries.register: everyday — casual and social; a business appointment is a meeting, not a meetup
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, an arranged social get-together. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so no passive exists: ✗ was met up at the taco place. Use plain meet if you need one: we were met at the gate.
entries.see also: meet up with, meet with, run into

entries.meaning: To join somebody somewhere by arrangement.
examples: I'm going to meet up with my cousin in Chicago.
She met up with the rest of the crew at the trailhead.
We'll meet up with you after the second set.
He had met up with them twice that week already.
Text me when you land and I'll meet up with you at baggage claim.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the person follows the whole phrase. ✗ met my cousin up with, ✗ met him up with; it is met up with him.
entries.register: everyday — casual, and only for planned meetings; a chance encounter is run into
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a planned joining-up with somebody; never a chance encounter, which is run into.
entries.passive: no — ✗ my cousin was met up with in Chicago, ✗ they had been met up with twice. Recast with plain meet: she was met at baggage claim.
entries.see also: meet up, meet with, run into

entries.meaning: To hold a formal meeting with somebody, or to receive a particular kind of response.
examples: The governor met with tribal leaders on Monday.
She meets with her advisor every other Thursday.
We have met with three contractors and liked none of them.
The proposal met with stiff resistance from the neighbors.
His first novel met with almost no success.
Her plan finally met with the board's approval.
Should the shipment meet with an accident, call the insurer that day.

senses.head: Hold a meeting with
body: The standard American business and political use, where the meeting is scheduled and has a purpose. (встречаться с, проводить встречу с)
examples: The governor met with tribal leaders on Monday.
She meets with her advisor every other Thursday.
We have met with three contractors and liked none of them.

senses.head: Receive, be greeted by (a response)
body: A fixed set of nouns follows: approval, resistance, opposition, success, an accident. The subject is a plan or a person, and the noun is what came back. (встретить, натолкнуться на; потерпеть (неудачу))
examples: The proposal met with stiff resistance from the neighbors.
His first novel met with almost no success.
Her plan finally met with the board's approval.
Should the shipment meet with an accident, call the insurer that day.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.русский: встречаться с (по делу); встретить, натолкнуться на (одобрение, сопротивление)
entries.separable: no — with never leaves its object: met with the union, met with them. ✗ met the union with.
entries.register: everyday in American English; British English drops the with for the appointment sense and simply says meet the client
entries.verb type: both — action in sense 1, an agentive scheduled meeting (the governor met with tribal leaders). Sense 2 is non-agentive and near-stative: the subject undergoes a reception rather than doing anything.
entries.passive: no in either sense — ✗ tribal leaders were met with on Monday, ✗ stiff resistance was met with by the proposal. Do not be fooled by the proposal was met with resistance: that is the passive of plain transitive meet plus a with phrase, not of this verb.
entries.see also: meet up with, run into, put forward

entries.meaning: To return money you owe, or to get even with somebody.
examples: I'll pay back the forty dollars on Friday.
She paid the loan back two years early.
Pay me back whenever you can.
He paid her back for every remark she ever made about his driving.
They paid the whole department back by leaking the memo.
She swore she would pay him back someday.

senses.head: Repay money
body: The object can be the sum, the loan, or the person you owe. (вернуть долг, отдать деньги)
examples: I'll pay back the forty dollars on Friday.
She paid the loan back two years early.
Pay me back whenever you can.

senses.head: Get even with somebody
body: The object is a person, and for introduces the offense. Often in the noun payback. (отомстить, отплатить)
examples: He paid her back for every remark she ever made about his driving.
They paid the whole department back by leaking the memo.
She swore she would pay him back someday.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun payback moves it forward, PAY-back
entries.русский: вернуть долг, отдать деньги; отомстить, отплатить
entries.separable: yes — pay back the loan or pay the loan back, and a pronoun must go in the middle: pay it back, pay me back, never ✗ pay back it.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object — either the money or the person
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, repaying money and getting even. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, with either object promoted — the loan was paid back two years early; she was paid back for every remark she ever made.
entries.see also: pay off, pay up, make up for

entries.meaning: To reduce a debt by paying part of it, without necessarily clearing it.
examples: We're trying to pay down the credit card before the rate resets.
She paid the balance down to under a thousand.
Every extra check pays it down a little faster.
The city has paid down half of its pension shortfall.
He paid the principal down for six years and then refinanced.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — pay down the mortgage or pay the mortgage down, and a pronoun must split the pair: pay it down, never ✗ pay down it.
entries.register: everyday — American money talk; a British paper is likelier to write pay off or reduce
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and gradual by definition, so the progressive is natural: we're paying the card down before the rate resets.
entries.passive: yes — the balance was paid down to under a thousand, half of the pension shortfall has been paid down.
entries.see also: pay off, pay back, run up

entries.meaning: To hand over money for something — and, idiomatically, to suffer the consequences of something.
examples: Her parents paid for the whole wedding.
The grant pays for two more technicians.
You'll pay for that remark.
He paid for the extra beers with a whole ruined Sunday.
The team paid for a slow first quarter.
She has paid for that decision every day since.
The new furnace paid for itself in three winters.

senses.head: Buy, settle the cost of
body: The plain money sense, which is transparent enough on its own but sets up everything below. (платить за, оплачивать)
examples: Her parents paid for the whole wedding.
The grant pays for two more technicians.

senses.head: Suffer the consequences
body: No money changes hands. The object is a mistake or a piece of bad behavior, and the tone is usually a threat or a warning. (поплатиться за, расплачиваться за)
examples: You'll pay for that remark.
He paid for the extra beers with a whole ruined Sunday.
The team paid for a slow first quarter.
She has paid for that decision every day since.

senses.head: Pay for itself
body: A fixed idiom: the thing saves enough money to cover what it cost. (окупаться, окупить себя)
examples: The new furnace paid for itself in three winters.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb and for reduces to /fɚ/
entries.separable: no — for keeps its object: paid for the tickets, paid for them. ✗ paid the tickets for.
entries.verb type: both — action in sense 1, an agentive handing over of money. Sense 2 is non-agentive, the subject suffering a consequence, and sense 3 (pay for itself) is a fixed reflexive idiom with an inanimate subject.
entries.passive: restricted — excellent in sense 1: the whole wedding was paid for by her parents, two more technicians are paid for by the grant. Sense 2 is marginal (?that remark will be paid for) and sense 3 has none, being reflexive: ✗ itself was paid for by the furnace.
entries.see also: pay off, pay up, run up

entries.meaning: To clear a debt completely, to bribe somebody, or — with no object — to turn out to have been worth it.
examples: They paid off the house in eleven years.
She paid the last card off in March.
Once you pay it off, the title comes in the mail.
Somebody had paid off the inspector.
You can't pay a jury off in a town this size.
All those early mornings finally paid off.
The gamble on a second location has paid off.
Half the yard staff were paid off when the contract ended.

senses.head: Clear a debt in full
body: The difference from pay down is completeness: you pay down a balance but pay off a loan. (выплатить полностью, погасить)
examples: They paid off the house in eleven years.
She paid the last card off in March.
Once you pay it off, the title comes in the mail.

senses.head: Bribe
body: Informal, and always shady — the object is the person being bought. (подкупить, дать взятку)
examples: Somebody had paid off the inspector.
You can't pay a jury off in a town this size.

senses.head: Produce a result, prove worth it
body: Intransitive, with the effort or the gamble as the subject. (окупиться, дать результат, оправдать себя)
examples: All those early mornings finally paid off.
The gamble on a second location has paid off.

senses.head: Dismiss with severance
body: British, and dated even there; American English says lay off or buy out. (рассчитать, уволить с выходным пособием)
examples: Half the yard staff were paid off when the contract ended.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a payoff moves it forward, PAY-off
entries.русский: полностью выплатить (долг); дать результат, окупиться; подкупить
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — pay off the mortgage or pay the mortgage off, and a pronoun must separate them: pay it off, never ✗ pay off it. Sense 3 has no object, so nothing moves there.
entries.register: everyday; the bribery sense is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: clearing a debt, bribing, dismissing with severance, and, in intransitive sense 3, an effort finally yielding a result.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the house was paid off in eleven years, the inspector had been paid off, half the yard staff were paid off when the contract ended. Sense 3 is intransitive: ✗ the gamble was paid off.
entries.see also: pay back, pay down, pay up

entries.meaning: To hand over a sum of money, usually a large or scheduled one, or to let out a rope little by little.
examples: The policy paid out about ninety thousand dollars.
The fund pays the interest out twice a year.
They refused to pay it out until the report was filed.
A machine that never pays out stops getting played.
He paid out another ten feet of line.
Pay the cable out slowly or it will kink.

senses.head: Disburse money
body: Insurers, funds, and lotteries pay out; the object is the sum or the claim. (выплачивать, выдавать (сумму))
examples: The policy paid out about ninety thousand dollars.
The fund pays the interest out twice a year.
They refused to pay it out until the report was filed.
A machine that never pays out stops getting played.

senses.head: Let out rope or cable
body: Nautical and technical: you feed the line slowly rather than releasing it. (травить, разматывать (трос))
examples: He paid out another ten feet of line.
Pay the cable out slowly or it will kink.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a payout moves it forward, PAY-out
entries.separable: yes — pay out the settlement or pay the settlement out, and a pronoun must go in the middle: pay it out, never ✗ pay out it.
entries.transitive: yes, though it is often used with no object stated when the subject is an insurer
entries.register: everyday in the money sense; the rope sense is nautical
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, disbursing a sum and feeding out rope; the money sense often leaves the object unstated (a machine that never pays out).
entries.passive: yes — about ninety thousand dollars was paid out on the policy; the cable was paid out slowly so it would not kink.
entries.see also: pay off, pay up, pay back

entries.meaning: To hand over money you owe, especially after being made to.
examples: The insurer took eight months to pay up.
Pay up or we take the car.
He lost the bet and paid up without a word.
Two of the tenants still haven't paid up.
She had paid up by the time the letter arrived.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the verb takes no object here, so no word can come between pay and up. ✗ pay the money up.
entries.register: everyday — often a demand, and slightly aggressive
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and usually a demand; the bare imperative pay up is its commonest form.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, so nothing can be promoted: ✗ the money was paid up, ✗ the tenants were paid up. Use pay off or pay back when a passive is needed.
entries.see also: pay off, pay back, pay out

entries.meaning: To communicate an idea so that people actually take it in.
examples: She put across a difficult argument in ten minutes.
He never quite put his point across to the committee.
The slides help, but you still have to put it across yourself.
A good teacher can put the same idea across three different ways.
The ad put across exactly the wrong message.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress, not the verb
entries.separable: yes — put across an idea or put the idea across, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put it across, never ✗ put across it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a verb of getting an idea to land. Often with can / could, but freely progressive: she's putting it across well.
entries.passive: yes — a difficult argument was put across in ten minutes, his point was never quite put across to the committee.
entries.see also: put forward, make out, put down to

entries.meaning: To save something for later, or to set a feeling or a disagreement out of the way.
examples: They put aside two hundred dollars a month.
She put a little aside every payday for years.
I put it aside for whoever needs it first.
The two families put aside a thirty-year quarrel for the funeral.
Put your doubts aside and read the whole thing first.
If we can put that question aside, the rest is simple.

senses.head: Save, set by for later
body: Money, time, a portion of something. (откладывать, копить)
examples: They put aside two hundred dollars a month.
She put a little aside every payday for years.
I put it aside for whoever needs it first.

senses.head: Set a feeling or a dispute out of the way
body: Differences, grudges, pride, doubts. (оставить в стороне, забыть о (разногласиях))
examples: The two families put aside a thirty-year quarrel for the funeral.
Put your doubts aside and read the whole thing first.
If we can put that question aside, the rest is simple.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — put aside some money or put some money aside, and a pronoun must separate the pair: put it aside, never ✗ put aside it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, setting money by and shelving a feeling or a dispute. No stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes — two hundred dollars was put aside every month; a thirty-year quarrel was put aside for the funeral.
entries.see also: put by, put off, put away

entries.meaning: To return something to where it belongs — and, in looser senses, to lock somebody up or to eat an alarming amount.
examples: Put away your tools before it rains.
She put the winter coats away in April.
Nobody puts them away except me.
The testimony put him away for nine years.
They put her away in a state hospital in 1953.
That kid can put away three plates of spaghetti.
He put a whole pie away by himself.

senses.head: Return to its place, tidy away
body: The core sense: the thing goes back to the drawer, the shelf, or the closet. (убрать на место, спрятать)
examples: Put away your tools before it rains.
She put the winter coats away in April.
Nobody puts them away except me.

senses.head: Lock up, imprison or commit
body: Informal, usually with a length of time. (упрятать, посадить (в тюрьму, в лечебницу))
examples: The testimony put him away for nine years.
They put her away in a state hospital in 1953.

senses.head: Consume a large quantity
body: Informal and admiring, almost always about food or drink. (умять, уговорить (много еды))
examples: That kid can put away three plates of spaghetti.
He put a whole pie away by himself.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress — put it aWAY, not PUT it away
entries.русский: убрать на место; упрятать (в тюрьму); умять (много еды)
entries.separable: yes — put away the dishes or put the dishes away, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put them away, never ✗ put away them.
entries.register: everyday; the eating and prison senses are informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses: tidying, imprisoning or committing, and eating a great deal.
entries.passive: yes — the winter coats were put away in April; he was put away for nine years; and informally a whole pie was put away in one sitting.
entries.see also: put aside, put up, put down

entries.meaning: To return something to where it was, to push a schedule later, to set a clock backward, or — informally — to drink something down fast.
examples: Put the milk back before it warms up.
He read two pages and put it back on the shelf.
Somebody put back an empty carton.
The hearing was put back to October.
They put the launch back another quarter.
Don't forget to put the clocks back on Sunday.
We put them back an hour and it was dark by five.
He put back two beers before the food came.
She can put three of those back and still walk a straight line.

senses.head: Return to its former place
body: The most common sense by far. (поставить обратно, вернуть на место)
examples: Put the milk back before it warms up.
He read two pages and put it back on the shelf.
Somebody put back an empty carton.

senses.head: Delay, move to a later time
body: More common in British English; Americans usually say push back or move back. (отложить, перенести на более поздний срок)
examples: The hearing was put back to October.
They put the launch back another quarter.

senses.head: Set a clock to an earlier time
body: What happens every autumn, when the clocks go back an hour. (перевести назад (часы))
examples: Don't forget to put the clocks back on Sunday.
We put them back an hour and it was dark by five.

senses.head: Drink quickly
body: Informal, and always with a counted quantity of drink. (опрокинуть, залпом выпить)
examples: He put back two beers before the food came.
She can put three of those back and still walk a straight line.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.русский: поставить обратно; отложить, отодвинуть (срок); перевести назад (часы); опрокинуть (стакан)
entries.separable: yes — put back the book or put the book back, and a pronoun must separate them: put it back, never ✗ put back it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: returning a thing, pushing a date later, resetting a clock, and drinking fast.
entries.passive: yes — the hearing was put back to October, the clocks are put back on Sunday, an empty carton had been put back on the shelf.
entries.see also: put off, put away, put forward

entries.meaning: To save money for a future need.
examples: She had put by enough to cover a bad winter.
They put a few dollars by every week for forty years.
Whatever he put by went into a coffee can.
There was nothing put by when the mill closed.
He put it by and never touched it again.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — put by a little money or put a little money by, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put it by, never ✗ put by it.
entries.register: rare — old-fashioned and mostly British; an American says put aside or save up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, a repeated act of saving against a future need. Old-fashioned and mostly British; no stative or linking use.
entries.passive: yes, though most often as a bare participle — there was nothing put by when the mill closed, enough had been put by to cover a bad winter.
entries.see also: put aside, pay down

entries.meaning: To set something down — and, in a family of idiomatic senses, to belittle, to euthanize, to suppress, to record, or to pay a deposit.
examples: Put the box down before you drop it.
She put down her fork and stared at him.
He puts everybody down and calls it honesty.
She never put her staff down in front of a client.
The vet said it was time to put him down.
They had to put the old horse down in the spring.
The army put down the rebellion in a week.
Put me down for twenty dollars.
She put down her maiden name by mistake.
They put down ten percent on the house.
We put two thousand down and financed the rest.

senses.head: Set down, stop holding
body: The literal core. (положить, поставить)
examples: Put the box down before you drop it.
She put down her fork and stared at him.

senses.head: Belittle, criticize
body: The object is a person; the noun putdown is the insult itself. (унижать, принижать, осаживать)
examples: He puts everybody down and calls it honesty.
She never put her staff down in front of a client.

senses.head: Euthanize an animal
body: The standard, gentle way to say it in American English. (усыпить (животное))
examples: The vet said it was time to put him down.
They had to put the old horse down in the spring.

senses.head: Suppress a revolt
body: Formal, historical. (подавить (восстание, мятеж))
examples: The army put down the rebellion in a week.

senses.head: Write down, record
body: Names, numbers, an amount on a list. (записать, внести (в список))
examples: Put me down for twenty dollars.
She put down her maiden name by mistake.

senses.head: Pay a deposit
body: With the money as the object, and often on plus the thing being bought. (внести (первоначальный взнос))
examples: They put down ten percent on the house.
We put two thousand down and financed the rest.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a putdown moves it forward, PUT-down
entries.русский: положить; унижать, принижать; усыпить (животное); подавить (восстание); записать
entries.separable: yes — put down the box or put the box down, and a pronoun must separate the pair: put it down, never ✗ put down it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all six senses: setting down, belittling, euthanizing, suppressing, recording, and paying a deposit. The noun a putdown comes from sense 2.
entries.passive: yes, and very common — the rebellion was put down in a week, the old horse was put down in the spring, her maiden name was put down by mistake, ten percent was put down on the house.
entries.see also: put down to, put up, put away, run down

entries.meaning: To explain something by naming its cause, usually a small or forgivable one.
examples: I put the mix-up down to a bad phone line.
She put his rudeness down to nerves.
Most of the drop can be put down to the weather.
Don't put it down to luck — she worked for it.
The coach put the loss down to one bad quarter.
They put the whole misunderstanding down to the late hour.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle; to is reduced to /tə/
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily so — the thing being explained sits between put and down, and the cause follows to: put the mistake down to fatigue, put it down to nerves. ✗ put down the mistake to fatigue, ✗ put down to it nerves. Only run by behaves the same way in this file; ordinary three-part verbs like put up with never split.
entries.transitive: yes, and it needs both an object and a to phrase
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, the act of assigning a cause. The progressive is fine: I'm putting it down to nerves.
entries.passive: yes — the entry's own example shows it: most of the drop can be put down to the weather; likewise his rudeness was put down to nerves.
entries.see also: put down, make of, read into

entries.meaning: To offer an idea, a plan, or a name for consideration.
examples: The department put forward three candidates.
She put her own name forward for the chair.
No one put it forward seriously until last year.
The theory was first put forward in 1911.
Clocks are put forward an hour in March.
They put the deadline forward by two weeks and everyone panicked.

senses.head: Propose an idea or a name
body: The main sense: something is placed in front of a group to be judged. (выдвигать, предлагать (на рассмотрение))
examples: The department put forward three candidates.
She put her own name forward for the chair.
No one put it forward seriously until last year.
The theory was first put forward in 1911.

senses.head: Move a clock or a date earlier
body: Chiefly British; Americans say move up. (перевести вперёд (часы); перенести на более ранний срок)
examples: Clocks are put forward an hour in March.
They put the deadline forward by two weeks and everyone panicked.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — put forward a proposal or put a proposal forward, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put it forward, never ✗ put forward it.
entries.register: formal — meetings, papers, and politics; in casual speech Americans say suggest or float
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive in both senses, proposing something for judgment and moving a clock or a date earlier. Formal register.
entries.passive: yes, and in writing the passive is the usual shape — the theory was first put forward in 1911, clocks are put forward an hour in March.
entries.see also: put across, put in for, put back

entries.meaning: To install something, to submit it, to contribute time and effort, or to slip a remark into a conversation.
examples: We put in a new water heater last fall.
They put the whole kitchen in over one weekend.
It took two men to put it in.
She put in a claim the day after the storm.
He put his notice in on a Tuesday.
He put in twelve years at the plant.
She puts in sixty hours a week during tax season.
"Not on Sunday," she put in.
He put in a word for her with the hiring manager.
The boat put in at Norfolk for repairs.
They put in at the first harbor with a working radio.

senses.head: Install, fit
body: Appliances, floors, windows, a pool. (установить, поставить, врезать)
examples: We put in a new water heater last fall.
They put the whole kitchen in over one weekend.
It took two men to put it in.

senses.head: Submit officially
body: A claim, an order, an application, a request. (подать (заявку, требование))
examples: She put in a claim the day after the storm.
He put his notice in on a Tuesday.

senses.head: Contribute time or effort
body: Hours, years, work. (вложить, отработать (время, силы))
examples: He put in twelve years at the plant.
She puts in sixty hours a week during tax season.

senses.head: Interject, add a remark
body: The remark itself is the object, and in reported speech it stands in front of the verb rather than after it. (вставить (слово), вставить замечание)
examples: "Not on Sunday," she put in.
He put in a word for her with the hiring manager.

senses.head: Of a boat, to stop at a port
body: Nautical and intransitive, always with at plus the place. (зайти в порт, зайти в гавань)
examples: The boat put in at Norfolk for repairs.
They put in at the first harbor with a working radio.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.русский: установить; подать (заявление); вложить (время, силы); вставить (слово); зайти в порт
entries.separable: yes — put in a new sink or put a new sink in, and a pronoun must separate them: put it in, never ✗ put in it.
entries.transitive: either — sense 5, the nautical one, takes no object
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: installing, submitting, contributing hours, interjecting a remark, and (intransitively, of a boat) stopping at a port.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — a new water heater was put in last fall, a claim was put in the day after the storm, twelve years were put in at the plant. Sense 5 is intransitive: ✗ Norfolk was put in at.
entries.see also: put in for, put up, put together

entries.meaning: To apply formally for something at work.
examples: She put in for two weeks in August.
He put in for the supervisor job and got it.
Three people put in for the same shift.
If you want the transfer, put in for it before Friday.
I had already put in for overtime that week.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — what you are applying for follows the whole phrase: put in for a transfer, put in for it. ✗ put a transfer in for, ✗ put it in for.
entries.register: everyday — workplace language, especially about leave, transfers, and overtime
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and agentive, applying formally at work; the subject is always a person.
entries.passive: no — the three-part prepositional passive fails: ✗ the transfer was put in for, ✗ overtime had been put in for by three people. Recast with apply for: the same shift was applied for by three people.
entries.see also: put in, put forward, pay out

entries.meaning: To move something to a later time, or to make somebody lose interest.
examples: They put off the wedding until spring.
We put the whole conversation off for a month.
Don't put it off any longer — just call.
He has put off going to the dentist since March.
The smell put me off before I even sat down.
His tone puts people off in the first minute.
She was put off by how quickly they wanted an answer.
I put the landlord off with a story about the mail.

senses.head: Postpone
body: The main sense, used of appointments, decisions, and chores. It also takes an -ing verb: put off calling her. (откладывать, переносить, оттягивать)
examples: They put off the wedding until spring.
We put the whole conversation off for a month.
Don't put it off any longer — just call.
He has put off going to the dentist since March.

senses.head: Repel, make someone lose interest
body: The object is a person, and the subject is whatever caused the reaction. The adjective off-putting comes from here. (отталкивать, вызывать неприязнь, отбивать охоту)
examples: The smell put me off before I even sat down.
His tone puts people off in the first minute.
She was put off by how quickly they wanted an answer.

senses.head: Fob off, get rid of for now
body: Putting a person off means stalling them rather than answering. (отделываться от, отговариваться)
examples: I put the landlord off with a story about the mail.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress — put it OFF, not PUT it off
entries.separable: yes — put off the meeting or put the meeting off, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put it off, never ✗ put off it. The same holds for the "repel" sense: it put me off, never ✗ it put off me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 3, postponing and stalling. Sense 2 is causative and non-agentive — the subject is whatever repels, not an actor — and gives the adjective off-putting.
entries.passive: yes — the wedding was put off until spring, going to the dentist has been put off since March; and sense 2 lives mainly in the passive: she was put off by how quickly they wanted an answer.
entries.see also: put back, put aside, put up with

entries.meaning: To dress in something, to switch something on, to gain weight, to stage a show, or to fool somebody.
examples: Put on a jacket — it's colder than it looks.
She put her boots on at the door.
Here's the hat; put it on.
Put the porch light on when you leave.
He put on the same record every night.
He put on fifteen pounds his first year away.
She put the weight on slowly and never noticed.
The high school puts on a musical every March.
They put a whole festival on with six volunteers.
You're putting me on — she really said that?
He puts on an accent whenever her family visits.

senses.head: Dress in, apply to the body
body: Clothes, shoes, sunscreen, a bandage. (надевать, наносить)
examples: Put on a jacket — it's colder than it looks.
She put her boots on at the door.
Here's the hat; put it on.

senses.head: Switch on, start playing
body: A light, the kettle, music, a game. (включать, ставить (музыку))
examples: Put the porch light on when you leave.
He put on the same record every night.

senses.head: Gain weight
body: With the amount or with weight as the object. (набирать (вес))
examples: He put on fifteen pounds his first year away.
She put the weight on slowly and never noticed.

senses.head: Stage, produce
body: Plays, concerts, exhibits, dinners. (ставить, устраивать (спектакль, мероприятие))
examples: The high school puts on a musical every March.
They put a whole festival on with six volunteers.

senses.head: Fool, tease
body: Informal American, nearly always in the progressive with a person as the object: you're putting me on. (разыгрывать, дурачить)
examples: You're putting me on — she really said that?

senses.head: Assume, feign
body: An accent, an air, a brave face. (напускать на себя, изображать)
examples: He puts on an accent whenever her family visits.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — put on your coat or put your coat on, and a pronoun must separate the pair: put it on, never ✗ put on it. That last point matters here: ✗ put on it is one of the most common errors in the whole group.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all six senses: dressing, switching on, gaining weight, staging a show, teasing, and feigning a manner.
entries.passive: yes in most senses — a musical is put on every March, the porch light was put on, you're being put on. The clothing sense passivizes only when somebody else does the dressing (the child's boots were put on for her); ?her boots were put on at the door is odd of a self-dresser.
entries.see also: put out, put up, put off

entries.meaning: To extinguish something, to issue it, to cause somebody trouble, or simply to set it outside.
examples: It took two crews to put the fire out.
Put your cigarette out before you come in.
She put it out with a dish towel.
The company put out a statement that afternoon.
They put three records out in one year.
I don't want to put you out.
Don't put yourself out on my account.
She was clearly put out that nobody had asked her first.
Put the trash out Sunday night.
She puts the cat out at bedtime and lets him back in at six.
The recycling goes Monday, so put it out Sunday evening.

senses.head: Extinguish
body: Fires, candles, cigarettes, lights. (тушить, гасить)
examples: It took two crews to put the fire out.
Put your cigarette out before you come in.
She put it out with a dish towel.

senses.head: Issue, publish, release
body: Statements, albums, reports, an APB. (выпускать, издавать, публиковать)
examples: The company put out a statement that afternoon.
They put three records out in one year.

senses.head: Inconvenience somebody
body: The object is a person; don't put yourself out is the polite formula. (причинять неудобство, утруждать)
examples: I don't want to put you out.
Don't put yourself out on my account.

senses.head: Be put out — be annoyed
body: Passive and adjectival, meaning mildly offended. (быть раздосадованным, обиженным)
examples: She was clearly put out that nobody had asked her first.

senses.head: Set outside
body: The plain literal sense, with the thing going out the door: the trash, the recycling, the cat. (выставлять (наружу), выносить)
examples: Put the trash out Sunday night.
She puts the cat out at bedtime and lets him back in at six.
The recycling goes Monday, so put it out Sunday evening.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.русский: тушить (огонь); выпускать, издавать; причинять неудобство; раздражённый (be put out); выставлять (наружу)
entries.separable: yes — put out the fire or put the fire out, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put it out, never ✗ put out it.
entries.transitive: yes — every sense here takes an object, though sense 4 is nearly always passive (be put out)
entries.register: everyday — be aware that put out also carries a vulgar slang sense (of a person, to consent to sex) that you should recognize and never produce
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1–3 and 5. Sense 4 is not a working verb but a participial adjective after a copula: she seemed put out, he looked put out.
entries.passive: yes — the fire was put out with a dish towel, a statement was put out that afternoon, the trash gets put out Sunday night. Sense 4 exists only in that passive shape: she was clearly put out that nobody had asked her.
entries.see also: put on, put up, put off

entries.meaning: To connect a phone call, to make somebody endure something, to pay for someone's schooling, or to get a deal completed.
examples: Can you put me through to billing?
She put the call through without asking who it was.
They put every recruit through the same week of tests.
He put his family through two years of that.
She waited tables and put herself through nursing school.
Their savings put both kids through college.
The bank put the loan through in three days.
They put through a rate increase in December.

senses.head: Connect by telephone
body: The object is the caller or the call; to names the destination. (соединить, перевести (звонок))
examples: Can you put me through to billing?
She put the call through without asking who it was.

senses.head: Make somebody endure something
body: Always with the person as the object and the ordeal after through. (подвергнуть, заставить пройти через)
examples: They put every recruit through the same week of tests.
He put his family through two years of that.

senses.head: Pay for someone's education
body: American and everyday: put her through college. (оплатить учёбу, выучить (кого-л.))
examples: She waited tables and put herself through nursing school.
Their savings put both kids through college.

senses.head: Get a deal or a measure completed
body: Business and legislative use. (провести, оформить (сделку, закон))
examples: The bank put the loan through in three days.
They put through a rate increase in December.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.русский: соединить (по телефону); подвергнуть (испытанию); оплатить учёбу; провести (сделку)
entries.separable: yes — put the call through or put through the call, and with a person as the object it always separates: put me through to sales, never ✗ put through me.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: connecting a call, making somebody endure an ordeal, funding an education, and getting a deal completed.
entries.passive: yes, and it is the normal form with a person as subject — I was put through to billing, every recruit is put through the same week of tests, the loan was put through in three days.
entries.see also: put up, put in, run through

entries.meaning: To assemble something out of parts, whether furniture, a plan, or a group of people.
examples: It took us four hours to put the crib together.
He put together the whole shed from a kit.
The instructions are useless — just put it together by eye.
She put together a proposal over the weekend.
They put a team together in less than a month.
He can put dinner together out of whatever is in the fridge.
She earns more than the other three put together.

senses.head: Assemble from parts
body: Furniture, engines, a puzzle. (собрать, смонтировать, сложить)
examples: It took us four hours to put the crib together.
He put together the whole shed from a kit.
The instructions are useless — just put it together by eye.

senses.head: Compile, organize
body: A plan, a proposal, a band, a meal, a case. (составить, подготовить, организовать)
examples: She put together a proposal over the weekend.
They put a team together in less than a month.
He can put dinner together out of whatever is in the fridge.

senses.head: All the rest put together
body: A fixed comparative tag meaning "combined." (вместе взятые)
examples: She earns more than the other three put together.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — put together a team or put a team together, and a pronoun must separate them: put it together, never ✗ put together it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, assembling from parts or compiling from scratch. Sense 3, the other three put together, is a frozen participial tag rather than a live verb.
entries.passive: yes — the crib was put together in four hours, the proposal was put together over the weekend, the whole shed was put together from a kit.
entries.see also: put up, put in, make up

entries.meaning: To erect something, to display it, to house somebody, to supply money, or to offer resistance.
examples: They put up a fence along the whole property line.
We put the tent up in the dark.
Help me put them up before the guests come.
Somebody put up a notice about the water shutoff.
They put us up for three nights.
Her cousin can put you up if the motel is full.
Two investors put up most of the money.
He put the bail up himself.
The old car put up a fight but the tow truck won.
They put up almost no resistance.
They put the house up for sale in July.

senses.head: Erect, build, hang
body: Tents, fences, sheds, shelves, decorations. (ставить, возводить, вешать)
examples: They put up a fence along the whole property line.
We put the tent up in the dark.
Help me put them up before the guests come.

senses.head: Display, post
body: Signs, notices, a flyer. (вывешивать, размещать)
examples: Somebody put up a notice about the water shutoff.

senses.head: Give somebody a place to stay
body: With the guest as the object. (приютить, разместить на ночь)
examples: They put us up for three nights.
Her cousin can put you up if the motel is full.

senses.head: Supply money
body: The object is the amount or the stake. (выложить, внести (деньги))
examples: Two investors put up most of the money.
He put the bail up himself.

senses.head: Offer resistance; make an effort
body: In the fixed phrases put up a fight, put up a struggle, put up a good show. (оказать (сопротивление), дать (бой))
examples: The old car put up a fight but the tow truck won.
They put up almost no resistance.

senses.head: Offer for sale; nominate
body: Put the house up for sale, put someone up for election. (выставить (на продажу); выдвинуть (кандидатуру))
examples: They put the house up for sale in July.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.русский: ставить, возводить; вывешивать; приютить; выложить (деньги); оказать (сопротивление)
entries.separable: yes — put up a tent or put a tent up, and a pronoun must go in the middle: put it up, never ✗ put up it. The same is true with people: put us up for the night.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense: erecting, posting a notice, housing a guest, supplying money, offering resistance, and putting something up for sale.
entries.passive: yes — a fence was put up along the property line, a notice was put up about the water shutoff, we were put up for three nights, most of the money was put up by two investors, the house was put up for sale in July.
entries.see also: put up with, put out, put together, run up

entries.meaning: To tolerate something annoying without complaining.
examples: I don't know how she puts up with that noise.
We put up with the delays for three years before anyone complained.
He has put up with worse.
She won't put up with being talked over.
You shouldn't have to put up with that.
Their neighbors put up with him for a decade.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle, not on the verb
entries.separable: no — the object always follows the whole phrase. ✗ put my neighbor up with, ✗ put it up with; it is put up with it.
entries.verb type: action in form — the progressive is fine, I'm putting up with it for now — though what it reports is closer to a state of tolerating than to anything done.
entries.passive: restricted — possible but stiff, and best with an inanimate subject: that kind of noise should not have to be put up with. ?He was put up with for a decade is grammatical but unidiomatic; Americans recast with tolerate.
entries.see also: put off, put upon, ride out

entries.meaning: To impose on somebody's good nature.
examples: She felt put upon every time the schedule came out.
The quieter staff are always the ones put upon.
Nobody likes being put upon by a stranger.
He was put upon for years and never said a word.
Ask, don't assume — she is easily put upon.
entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.русский: злоупотреблять чьей-л. добротой; чувствовать себя используемым
entries.separable: no — upon keeps its object: put upon her, ✗ put her upon. In practice you will almost only meet the passive participle, feel put upon.
entries.transitive: yes, but nearly always in the passive
entries.register: formal — old-fashioned, and mostly met as the fixed participle feel put upon; for the active idea Americans say take advantage of
entries.verb type: action in form, but it survives almost only as a participial adjective after a copula — feel put upon, seem put upon. The active put upon her is formal and rare.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is effectively the only living form — he was put upon for years and never said a word, nobody likes being put upon by a stranger, she is easily put upon.
entries.see also: put up with, put out

entries.meaning: To abandon somebody, or to stop working just when somebody needed you.
examples: Don't quit on me now — we're two miles from the car.
Half the roster quit on the coach by November.
He never quit on his brother, not once.
The truck quit on me at the light.
My laptop had quit on her right before the deadline.
Two of the space heaters quit on us that winter.

senses.head: Abandon somebody, give up on them
body: The reproach is built in: you did not just leave, you left them. (бросить, подвести, махнуть рукой на)
examples: Don't quit on me now — we're two miles from the car.
Half the roster quit on the coach by November.
He never quit on his brother, not once.

senses.head: Stop working (of a machine)
body: The device is the subject and the owner is the victim. (отказать, заглохнуть)
examples: The truck quit on me at the light.
My laptop had quit on her right before the deadline.
Two of the space heaters quit on us that winter.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.русский: подвести, бросить (в трудный момент); отказать (о технике)
entries.separable: no — on keeps its object, which is always a person: quit on me, quit on the team. ✗ quit me on.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after on
entries.register: informal — spoken American English, common in sports and in talk about broken machinery
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, a person walking out on somebody and a machine failing at the worst moment. Informal spoken American.
entries.passive: no — ✗ the coach was quit on by half the roster, ✗ I was quit on by the truck. The verb is fixed in the active, with the person let down after on.
entries.see also: run out on, run out, pay off

entries.meaning: To read aloud something just written down or heard, so that it can be checked.
examples: Could you read back the confirmation number?
She read the address back to make sure she had it right.
Read it back to me one more time.
The clerk read back the witness's last answer.
The tower asked him to read the clearance back.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; in the past the verb is said /rɛd/, red-BACK
entries.separable: yes — read back the number or read the number back, and a pronoun must go in the middle: read it back, never ✗ read back it.
entries.register: everyday — the standard word on phones, in cockpits, and in courtrooms
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, reading something aloud so it can be checked; standard on the phone, in cockpits, and in courtrooms.
entries.passive: yes — the witness's last answer was read back, the clearance has to be read back to the tower.
entries.see also: read out, read off, read over

entries.meaning: To find a meaning in something that was probably never there.
examples: Don't read too much into one bad review.
She read a promise into what was only politeness.
People read whatever they want into that painting.
I wouldn't read anything into the delay.
Analysts read far more into the phrasing than the author intended.
She only asked how you were — don't read anything into it.
entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb; into reduces to /ˈɪntə/
entries.русский: видеть (в чём-л.) больше, чем есть; домысливать
entries.type: prepositional verb, in the frame read something into something
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily so — how much you are reading is the object of read and sits in front of into, with the thing being read after it: read too much into her silence, don't read anything into it. ✗ read into her silence too much. Into itself never lets go of what follows, so a pronoun there stays behind it: read nothing into it, never ✗ read it into nothing.
entries.transitive: yes, and it needs both an object and an into phrase
entries.verb type: action — dynamic but mental, finding a meaning that was probably never there. Usually negative or with too much.
entries.passive: restricted — only the quantity phrase can be promoted: too much has been read into one bad review, far more was read into the phrasing than the author intended. ✗ her silence was read into, because into keeps its own object.
entries.see also: make of, put down to, read out

entries.meaning: To read a figure or an item aloud from a display, a label, or a list.
examples: Read off the numbers and I'll write them down.
He read the meter off to the dispatcher.
She read them off one at a time.
The nurse read off his blood pressure without looking up.
Just read the code off the back of the router.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — read off the serial number or read the serial number off, and a pronoun must separate them: read it off, never ✗ read off it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. A physical act of reading aloud off a display or a label, so the progressive is natural: she was reading off the serial numbers as he typed.
entries.passive: yes, and it is common in reports of procedure: the numbers were read off one at a time, his blood pressure was read off without comment.
entries.see also: read out, read back, make out

entries.meaning: To read something aloud to a group.
examples: The judge read out the verdict at four.
She read the whole list out twice.
Read it out so everyone can hear.
He read out the names of the graduating class.
They read the terms out before anyone signed.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a readout moves it forward, REED-out
entries.separable: yes — read out the names or read the names out, and a pronoun must go in the middle: read them out, never ✗ read out them.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Reading aloud to a group, an event with a beginning and an end: the clerk was reading out the names when we came in.
entries.passive: yes, and very natural — this is the standard way to report it: the verdict was read out at four, the terms were read out before anyone signed.
entries.see also: read off, read back, read over

entries.meaning: To read something once through in order to check it.
examples: Read the contract over before you sign anything.
She read it over twice and still missed the date.
He read over my cover letter and cut two paragraphs.
Read your answers over if there's time left.
The lawyer read over the clause and shook her head.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — read over the contract or read the contract over, and a pronoun must separate the pair: read it over, never ✗ read over it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Checking something by reading it once through, a deliberate act: she was reading over the contract when he called.
entries.passive: yes — the contract was read over twice before anyone signed, my cover letter was read over and cut by two paragraphs.
entries.see also: read through, run over, read out

entries.meaning: To read something from beginning to end.
examples: I read through the whole manual and learned nothing.
She read the draft through on the train.
Read it through once before you start marking it up.
He had read through every file by midnight.
The cast read through the script on the first morning.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a read-through moves it forward, REED-throo
entries.русский: прочитать целиком, прочесть от начала до конца
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle) — through also works as a plain preposition here
entries.separable: yes — read through the draft or read the draft through, and read it through is standard. This one is unusual: because through doubles as a preposition, read through it is equally good, which is not true of ordinary particles (✗ read out them).
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. A single complete pass from beginning to end, so it is often perfective: I had read through the whole manual by midnight.
entries.passive: yes — the script was read through on the first morning, every file had been read through by midnight.
entries.see also: read over, run through, read up on

entries.meaning: To study a subject on your own before you need to know it.
examples: I read up on the neighborhood before we made an offer.
She read up on the procedure the night before.
He read up on it enough to sound convincing.
Read up on the tax rules before you file that.
They had read up on every candidate by October.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the subject matter follows the whole phrase: read up on the surgery, read up on it. ✗ read the surgery up on, ✗ read it up on.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic. Deliberate private study over a stretch of time: she was reading up on the procedure all week.
entries.passive: restricted — the three-part frame passivizes stiffly. ?the tax rules were read up on before he filed is grammatical but nobody says it; ✗ it was read up on by her is worse. Keep it active.
entries.see also: read through, read over, run through

entries.meaning: To depend on something, with a great deal at stake.
examples: A lot is riding on Thursday's vote.
Her whole season was riding on one throw.
Three hundred jobs are riding on the contract.
Nothing much rides on it either way.
With that much money riding on the outcome, nobody slept.
entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.русский: зависеть от, быть поставленным на карту
entries.separable: no — on keeps its object: riding on this game, riding on it. ✗ ride this game on.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after on
entries.register: everyday — usually in the progressive, with an amount or a stake as the subject
entries.verb type: stative in meaning — it names a relation of dependency, not an act: a lot rides on Thursday's vote. Unusually for a stative it prefers the progressive, which here marks the state, not an activity: three hundred jobs are riding on the contract.
entries.passive: no — the subject is the stake and on will not release its object: ✗ Thursday's vote is being ridden on by a lot, ✗ the contract is ridden on by three hundred jobs.
entries.see also: ride out, run on, rise to

entries.meaning: To get through a bad stretch without being destroyed by it, usually by waiting rather than acting.
examples: They rode out the hurricane in the basement.
The firm rode the recession out on two contracts.
There's nothing to do but ride it out.
She rode out the scandal and kept her seat.
Small boats can ride a squall out if the anchor holds.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: yes — ride out the storm or ride the storm out, and a pronoun must go in the middle: ride it out, never ✗ ride out it.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, though what it describes is endurance rather than activity: you ride out a storm by waiting: they were riding out the hurricane in the basement.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical but stiff, and the active is overwhelmingly preferred: ?the recession was ridden out on two contracts, ?the scandal was ridden out. Say they rode it out.
entries.see also: put up with, ride on, rise above

entries.meaning: Of a garment, to work its way upward out of place.
examples: This skirt rides up every time I sit down.
His shirt had ridden up in the back all through the photos.
Cheap leggings ride up at the knee.
The strap kept riding up on her shoulder.
Wash it once and the hem rides up for good.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the clothing is the subject, not an object, so no word can come between ride and up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, with an inanimate subject that does the moving: the garment works its way upward on its own. Habitual present is the usual tense: this skirt rides up every time I sit down.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, with no object anywhere to promote: ✗ the knee is ridden up at by cheap leggings.
entries.see also: ride out, rise up

entries.meaning: To telephone somebody again, or to return their call.
examples: She's in a meeting; can she ring you back?
He rang back twice before lunch.
I'll ring the surgery back after four.
If the line drops, ring me back on the mobile.
Nobody had rung back by Friday.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the past is rang back /ræŋ/
entries.separable: yes — ring the office back is the usual order and ring back the office is possible, but with a pronoun the split is compulsory: ring me back, never ✗ ring back me.
entries.transitive: either — he'll ring back and he'll ring you back are both normal
entries.register: British — an American says call back, and would find ring me back noticeably English
entries.verb type: action — dynamic; the act of returning a call. Transitive or intransitive with no change of meaning: he'll ring back, he'll ring you back.
entries.passive: restricted — the transitive use will passivize in British English (she was rung back within the hour) but it is rare and the active is standard. No passive at all of the intransitive he rang back twice.
entries.see also: ring up, ring off, ring in

entries.meaning: To welcome something with bells or celebration, or — in British use — to phone your workplace.
examples: We rang in the new year on somebody's roof.
The town rings the new year in with a fish fry.
They rang it in quietly, with two candles and the radio.
Two of the drivers rang in sick.
He rang in to say the van had broken down.

senses.head: Ring in the new year
body: A fixed American phrase, from church bells at midnight, now used of any noisy celebration of a beginning. (встречать (Новый год), отмечать наступление)
examples: We rang in the new year on somebody's roof.
The town rings the new year in with a fish fry.
They rang it in quietly, with two candles and the radio.

senses.head: Phone in to work
body: British; the American equivalent is call in, as in call in sick. (позвонить на работу, сообщить по телефону)
examples: Two of the drivers rang in sick.
He rang in to say the van had broken down.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.русский: встречать (Новый год); позвонить и сообщить (на работу)
entries.separable: yes in sense 1 — ring in the new year or ring the new year in, and a pronoun goes in the middle: ring it in. Sense 2 takes no object at all.
entries.register: everyday in sense 1; sense 2 is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses — the celebratory ring in the new year and the British ring in sick are each things people do at a moment: they were ringing in the new year on the roof.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1, where there is an object: the new year was rung in with a fish fry. No in sense 2, which takes no object: ✗ sick was rung in by two of the drivers.
entries.see also: ring out, ring up, ring back

entries.meaning: To end a telephone call.
examples: She rang off before I could ask.
He rang off without saying goodbye.
I'd better ring off — someone's at the door.
They had rung off by the time I picked up the extension.
He rings off the moment the topic turns to money.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the verb takes no object, so no word can come between ring and off.
entries.register: British — and dated even there; Americans say hang up
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — a single punctual act, the end of a call: she rang off before I could ask. It takes the progressive only in the sense of being about to: I'm ringing off now.
entries.passive: no — objectless, so nothing can be promoted to subject: ✗ the call was rung off, ✗ I was rung off on.
entries.see also: ring back, ring up

entries.meaning: Of a sound, to carry loudly and clearly; and, in the old phrase, to see the old year off.
examples: A single shot rang out across the field.
Her laugh rang out over everyone else's.
The bells ring out every hour on the hour.
Three cheers had rung out before the doors even opened.
They ring the old year out and the new one in on the same bell.
At midnight the bells ring it out, and a minute later they start on the new one.

senses.head: Sound out loudly
body: Shots, bells, laughter, a voice. The sound is the subject and there is no object. (раздаться, прозвучать, разнестись)
examples: A single shot rang out across the field.
Her laugh rang out over everyone else's.
The bells ring out every hour on the hour.
Three cheers had rung out before the doors even opened.

senses.head: Ring out the old year
body: The other half of ring in the new year, and used almost only in that pairing. (провожать (старый год))
examples: They ring the old year out and the new one in on the same bell.
At midnight the bells ring it out, and a minute later they start on the new one.
