entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the past is rang out /ræŋ/
entries.separable: nothing to separate in sense 1, which takes no object. Sense 2 is a fixed phrase, and there the pronoun does split it: ring the old year out, ring it out.
entries.transitive: either — no object in sense 1, an object in sense 2
entries.register: everyday — sense 1 has a literary edge and turns up in news writing more often than in conversation
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in sense 1, with the sound itself as subject: a single shot rang out. Sense 2 (ring out the old year) is dynamic and transitive but frozen into that one phrase.
entries.passive: no in sense 1 — it has no object: ✗ the field was rung out across by a shot. Restricted in sense 2: the old year is rung out on the same bell is possible but ceremonial, and outside that phrase it does not occur.
entries.see also: ring in, ring up

entries.meaning: To enter a sale on a cash register, to rack up a total, or — in British English — to telephone somebody.
examples: She rang up two coffees and a muffin.
He rang the whole order up wrong.
Ring it up as a return, not a sale.
The team rang up thirty-one points in the first half.
The studio has rung up four straight hits.
He rang a thousand dollars up in penalties in one month.
Ring me up when you get in.

senses.head: Enter a sale on a register
body: From the bell of an old cash register. The object is the item or the amount. (пробить (на кассе), провести (покупку))
examples: She rang up two coffees and a muffin.
He rang the whole order up wrong.
Ring it up as a return, not a sale.

senses.head: Rack up a total
body: Extended from the register to any running total — points, wins, profits, charges. Common in American sports and business writing. (набрать, записать на свой счёт)
examples: The team rang up thirty-one points in the first half.
The studio has rung up four straight hits.
He rang a thousand dollars up in penalties in one month.

senses.head: Telephone
body: British; Americans say call. (позвонить, набрать номер)
examples: Ring me up when you get in.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the past is rang up /ræŋ/ and the participle rung up /rʌŋ/
entries.русский: пробить (на кассе); набрать, записать на свой счёт (очки, прибыль); позвонить (брит.)
entries.separable: yes — ring up the sale or ring the sale up, and a pronoun must go in the middle: ring it up, never ✗ ring up it. Same in the British telephone sense: ring me up.
entries.register: everyday in American English for senses 1 and 2; sense 3 is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — entering a sale, racking up a total, or (British) telephoning. All take the progressive: she was ringing up two coffees.
entries.passive: yes, and it is idiomatic in senses 1 and 2: the whole order was rung up wrong, thirty-one points were rung up in the first half. The British telephone sense passivizes only awkwardly: ?I was rung up by his office.
entries.see also: ring back, ring in, run up

entries.meaning: To refuse to be dragged down to the level of something petty, or to overcome a disadvantage.
examples: Whatever they post, rise above it.
She rose above the sniping and finished the report.
He has never once risen above an argument he could win.
Half the class rose above the neighborhood they grew up in.
The film rises above a very thin script.

senses.head: Refuse to stoop to something
body: Insults, gossip, provocation. Very often the bare advice rise above it. (быть выше (чего-л.), не опускаться до)
examples: Whatever they post, rise above it.
She rose above the sniping and finished the report.
He has never once risen above an argument he could win.

senses.head: Overcome a limitation or a start in life
body: Poverty, an injury, a bad reputation. (преодолеть, подняться над)
examples: Half the class rose above the neighborhood they grew up in.
The film rises above a very thin script.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.separable: no — above keeps its object: rise above it, rise above the insults. ✗ rise it above.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after above
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses, though nothing physical moves — refusing to stoop (rise above it) and overcoming a disadvantage (the film rises above a thin script) are both achievements rather than states.
entries.passive: no — rise is intransitive and above keeps its object: ✗ the sniping was risen above by her, ✗ a thin script is risen above by the film.
entries.see also: ride out, rise to, put up with

entries.meaning: To meet a demand well when it comes, or to take a piece of provocation.
examples: The whole crew rose to the occasion when the power failed.
Nobody expected a rookie to rise to that kind of pressure.
She has risen to every challenge they have handed her.
He posted it to get a reaction and half the room rose to it.
Don't rise to the bait — that is exactly what he wants.

senses.head: Rise to the occasion or the challenge
body: The complimentary sense: the moment was big and the person was equal to it. (оказаться на высоте, справиться)
examples: The whole crew rose to the occasion when the power failed.
Nobody expected a rookie to rise to that kind of pressure.
She has risen to every challenge they have handed her.

senses.head: Rise to the bait
body: The unflattering sense: taking an obvious provocation. (поддаться на, клюнуть на (провокацию))
examples: He posted it to get a reaction and half the room rose to it.
Don't rise to the bait — that is exactly what he wants.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb; to is reduced to /tə/
entries.separable: no — to keeps its object: rise to the occasion, rise to it. ✗ rise the occasion to.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after to
entries.register: everyday — mostly inside a short list of fixed objects: the occasion, the challenge, the bait
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — an achievement at a particular moment, whether creditable (rose to the occasion when the power failed) or not (half the room rose to it).
entries.passive: no — the verb is intransitive, so the object of to cannot move: ✗ the occasion was risen to by the whole crew, ✗ the bait was risen to.
entries.see also: rise above, ride on, run with

entries.meaning: To rebel against a power, or, more literally, to loom up in front of somebody.
examples: The provinces rose up against the new tax.
Whole towns rose up that spring.
He warned that people would rise up if the mine closed.
The ridge rises up out of flat country with no warning.
A wall of water had risen up behind the boat before anyone shouted.

senses.head: Rebel
body: With against naming what is being resisted. (восстать, подняться (против))
examples: The provinces rose up against the new tax.
Whole towns rose up that spring.
He warned that people would rise up if the mine closed.

senses.head: Loom, tower
body: Literary: a cliff, a wall, or a wave rising in front of you. (вздыматься, возвышаться)
examples: The ridge rises up out of flat country with no warning.
A wall of water had risen up behind the boat before anyone shouted.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the verb takes no object, so no word can come between rise and up.
entries.transitive: no, takes no object; the people or the thing rising are the subject
entries.register: everyday, with a formal and historical flavor — you meet it in speeches and history writing more than in conversation
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in the rebellion sense (the provinces rose up against the new tax). The literary sense 2 is closer to a stative description of landscape, in the habitual present: the ridge rises up out of flat country.
entries.passive: no — intransitive in both senses, with the rebels or the cliff as subject: ✗ the new tax was risen up against, ✗ flat country is risen up out of.
entries.see also: rise above, ride up, put up

entries.meaning: To find something or meet somebody by chance.
examples: I ran across an old photo of your mother in a library book.
She ran across the same typo in three different files.
We ran across him at a gas station in Nevada.
If you ever run across one of those, buy it.
He had run across the name twice that week and thought nothing of it.
entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.separable: no — across keeps its object: ran across an old photo, ran across it. ✗ ran an old photo across.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after across
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, but purely accidental and momentary, so the progressive is odd: ✗ I am running across an old photo. Use it in the simple past: I ran across it in a library book.
entries.passive: no — this is the textbook prepositional verb that will not passivize: ✗ an old photo was run across in a library book, ✗ he was run across at a gas station.
entries.see also: run into, make off with, run up against

entries.meaning: To chase somebody, or to pursue them romantically with more eagerness than dignity.
examples: He ran after the bus for half a block and gave up.
She ran after him with the receipt he had left on the counter.
He spent two years running after a woman who was never going to call back.
She has better things to do than run after anybody.
I'm not running after three grown men all weekend.
Somebody has to run after them and turn the lights off.

senses.head: Chase, pursue on foot
body: The literal sense — a bus, a dog, a child. (гнаться за, бежать за)
examples: He ran after the bus for half a block and gave up.
She ran after him with the receipt he had left on the counter.

senses.head: Pursue romantically
body: Always with a hint that the pursuer is making a fool of himself. (бегать за, добиваться (кого-л.))
examples: He spent two years running after a woman who was never going to call back.
She has better things to do than run after anybody.

senses.head: Wait on, clean up after
body: With the sense of constant unrewarded service. (бегать за, обслуживать)
examples: I'm not running after three grown men all weekend.
Somebody has to run after them and turn the lights off.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.separable: no — after keeps its object: ran after the bus, ran after him. ✗ ran the bus after, ✗ ran him after.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after after
entries.register: everyday; the romantic sense is informal and mildly disapproving
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — chasing on foot, pursuing romantically, and waiting on somebody — and all three take the progressive: he spent two years running after her.
entries.passive: restricted — the literal chase resists it (✗ the bus was run after for half a block), but the romantic sense passivizes in the abstract: she has no interest in being run after.
entries.see also: run around, run away with, run down

entries.meaning: To go away now, said kindly to a child and condescendingly to anybody else.
examples: Run along now, the bus is coming.
She told the kids to run along and let the grown-ups talk.
He waved us off — "run along, I've got this."
The children had run along before the argument really started.
"Run along," he said, and she understood exactly what he meant by it.
entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: nothing to separate — no object follows, so no word can come between run and along.
entries.register: informal — nearly always an imperative said to a child, and slightly dated; said to an adult it is a dismissal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and almost frozen in the imperative: run along now. Outside commands and reported commands it barely appears.
entries.passive: no — no object at all: ✗ the kids were run along, ✗ it was run along by the children.
entries.see also: run away, run off

entries.meaning: To rush from place to place accomplishing little, and, with a preposition, to keep somebody's company or to be unfaithful to them.
examples: I ran around all morning and got nothing crossed off.
She has been running around since six.
He runs around with a crowd his mother does not care for.
They ran around together the whole summer after high school.
Everyone in town knew he was running around on her.
The insurer gave us the runaround for six weeks.

senses.head: Rush about, be busy in all directions
body: Often with like a comparison — running around like a maniac. (носиться, суетиться, бегать туда-сюда)
examples: I ran around all morning and got nothing crossed off.
She has been running around since six.

senses.head: Run around with — spend time with
body: Of a crowd or a companion, usually with a raised eyebrow. (водиться с, якшаться с)
examples: He runs around with a crowd his mother does not care for.
They ran around together the whole summer after high school.

senses.head: Run around on — be unfaithful to
body: Informal American. (изменять (кому-л.))
examples: Everyone in town knew he was running around on her.

senses.head: Give somebody the runaround
body: The noun: to fob a person off with delays and transfers instead of an answer. (водить за нос, морочить голову)
examples: The insurer gave us the runaround for six weeks.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun the runaround moves it forward, RUN-uh-rownd
entries.русский: носиться, суетиться; водить за нос (the runaround)
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the verb takes no object here. The related expressions attach a preposition instead: run around with somebody, run around after somebody, run around on somebody.
entries.register: everyday; run around on (cheat on a spouse) is informal
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and characteristically progressive because it describes ongoing scattered activity: she has been running around since six.
entries.passive: no — the verb takes no object of its own: ✗ all morning was run around. Even the prepositional run around on somebody stays active: ✗ she was being run around on — say he was cheating on her.
entries.see also: run after, run away, run off with

entries.meaning: To leave a place you are supposed to stay in, or to avoid something instead of facing it.
examples: He ran away twice before he turned fifteen.
The dog ran away during the fireworks and turned up two days later.
She had run away to Reno at nineteen and stayed.
You can't run away from a bill like that forever.
He runs away from every conversation that matters.

senses.head: Flee, leave home
body: Children run away from home; animals run away. (убежать, сбежать (из дома))
examples: He ran away twice before he turned fifteen.
The dog ran away during the fireworks and turned up two days later.
She had run away to Reno at nineteen and stayed.

senses.head: Avoid instead of facing
body: With from plus a problem, a feeling, or a responsibility. (бежать от, уходить от (проблемы))
examples: You can't run away from a bill like that forever.
He runs away from every conversation that matters.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a runaway moves it forward, RUN-uh-way
entries.separable: nothing to separate — the verb takes no object. For the thing or person taken along, use run away with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses — fleeing a place (he ran away twice before fifteen) and avoiding a problem (he runs away from every conversation that matters).
entries.passive: no — intransitive throughout: ✗ home was run away from by him, ✗ a bill like that can't be run away from.
entries.see also: run away with, run off, run out on

entries.meaning: To leave with somebody or something you were not entitled to, to win something easily, or, of a feeling, to take charge of a person.
examples: She ran away with a bass player from Tulsa.
Somebody ran away with the whole tip jar.
The tide ran away with both of our chairs.
The visiting team ran away with it in the third quarter.
Her short film ran away with every prize that year.
Don't let your imagination run away with you.

senses.head: Elope with, leave with somebody
body: (сбежать с, убежать с)
examples: She ran away with a bass player from Tulsa.

senses.head: Take and go, steal
body: (унести, украсть, скрыться с)
examples: Somebody ran away with the whole tip jar.
The tide ran away with both of our chairs.

senses.head: Win easily
body: Sports and awards writing: the margin was never in doubt. (легко выиграть, унести (победу))
examples: The visiting team ran away with it in the third quarter.
Her short film ran away with every prize that year.

senses.head: Of a feeling, to take over
body: The fixed shape is let your imagination / your temper run away with you. (захлестнуть, взять верх над)
examples: Don't let your imagination run away with you.

entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.русский: сбежать с (кем-л.); унести, украсть; легко выиграть; захлестнуть (о чувствах)
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: ran away with the money, ran away with it. ✗ ran the money away with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses. Sense 4 is the odd one: the feeling is the subject and the person the object — don't let your imagination run away with you.
entries.passive: restricted, and marginal in practice: ✗ the whole tip jar was run away with, ✗ he was run away with by a bass player. Sports writing will occasionally allow the game was run away with in the third quarter, but the active is the safe choice.
entries.see also: run off with, make off with, run away

entries.meaning: To show somebody an idea and ask what they think before you act on it.
examples: Let me run it by my manager first.
She ran the whole plan by legal before anyone signed.
Run the numbers by me one more time.
Nobody ran the new logo by the people who have to use it.
He had run the offer by his wife before he called back.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress stays on the verb; by is unstressed
entries.type: three-part phrasal verb (verb + object + preposition), in the frame run something by somebody
entries.separable: yes, and obligatorily so — the thing you are showing sits between run and by, and the person follows: run the idea by her, run it by legal. ✗ run by her the idea. Run it past her works exactly the same way. The only other verb here that must split like this is put down to.
entries.transitive: yes, and it needs both an object and a by phrase
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — a deliberate act of consultation: I was running it by legal all last week. The frame needs both an object and a by phrase.
entries.passive: yes, and it is genuinely idiomatic in American workplace English: the plan was run by legal before anyone signed, has this been run by the client yet? The agent, when named, needs a second by: it was run by legal by his assistant — clumsy, so leave the agent out.
entries.see also: run through, put forward, run over

entries.meaning: To knock somebody down with a vehicle, to belittle them, to lose power, to track something down, or to go through a list.
examples: A pickup ran down two cyclists on the shoulder.
He ran the mailbox down backing out.
He runs everybody down and wonders why nobody calls.
She never ran her old firm down in an interview.
The battery had run down overnight.
The plant slowly ran down through the eighties.
It took a week to run down the original invoice.
She ran the rumor down to a single email.
Let me run down what we know so far.
He ran the schedule down twice and still forgot Thursday.
Run it down for me one more time — I lost the thread.

senses.head: Knock down with a vehicle
body: More violent than run over: the driver keeps going, and the word often implies intent. (сбить, задавить (машиной))
examples: A pickup ran down two cyclists on the shoulder.
He ran the mailbox down backing out.

senses.head: Belittle, criticize
body: The object is a person or their work. (ругать, принижать, охаивать)
examples: He runs everybody down and wonders why nobody calls.
She never ran her old firm down in an interview.

senses.head: Lose power, wind down
body: Intransitive, of batteries, clocks, and businesses. (разряжаться, садиться; приходить в упадок)
examples: The battery had run down overnight.
The plant slowly ran down through the eighties.

senses.head: Track down, locate
body: A source, a lead, a spare part. (разыскать, отследить)
examples: It took a week to run down the original invoice.
She ran the rumor down to a single email.

senses.head: Go through item by item
body: Usually a list, an agenda, or the numbers; the noun rundown is the summary itself. (перечислить, пробежаться по (списку))
examples: Let me run down what we know so far.
He ran the schedule down twice and still forgot Thursday.
Run it down for me one more time — I lost the thread.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a rundown moves it forward, RUN-down
entries.русский: сбить (машиной); ругать, принижать; разряжаться, садиться; разыскать; перечислить
entries.separable: yes — run down the list or run the list down, and a pronoun must go in the middle: run it down, never ✗ run down it. Sense 3 has no object at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout: hitting somebody with a vehicle, belittling them, tracking a thing down, or going through a list. Sense 3 (the battery had run down) is a dynamic change of state with the battery as subject.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses, and common in senses 1 and 4: two cyclists were run down on the shoulder, the original invoice was finally run down, she was run down by her own department. No passive of sense 3: ✗ the battery was run down overnight can only mean somebody drained it.
entries.see also: run over, run through, put down

entries.meaning: To be a candidate for an office.
examples: He plans to run for mayor next spring.
She ran for city council twice and lost both times.
No incumbent has run for reelection in this district since 2016.
Half the reason to run for anything is the mailing list.
When the siren went off we just ran for it.

senses.head: Be a candidate
body: The office follows for, with no article for the big ones: run for president, run for sheriff. (баллотироваться, выдвигать свою кандидатуру)
examples: He plans to run for mayor next spring.
She ran for city council twice and lost both times.
No incumbent has run for reelection in this district since 2016.
Half the reason to run for anything is the mailing list.

senses.head: Run for it
body: A separate fixed idiom: to make a dash for safety. (броситься наутёк, бежать со всех ног)
examples: When the siren went off we just ran for it.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb; for reduces to /fɚ/
entries.separable: no — for keeps its object: run for mayor, run for it. ✗ run mayor for.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after for
entries.register: everyday — the standard American political word; British English says stand for
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, and often durative — a whole campaign, not a moment: she is running for city council this spring. The fixed run for it (sense 2) is punctual instead.
entries.passive: no — the office cannot become the subject: ✗ mayor is being run for by him, ✗ reelection has not been run for since 2016.
entries.see also: run into, put forward, run up against

entries.meaning: To take somebody to the police station, or to break in a new engine gently.
examples: They ran him in for the third time that year.
The sergeant threatened to run the whole group in.
He got run in for something that would not even be a ticket now.
Run the engine in gently for the first thousand miles.
The manual says to run it in before towing anything.

senses.head: Arrest, haul in
body: Informal and old-fashioned — the language of black-and-white movies. The noun a run-in with somebody (an argument) is still completely current. (задержать, забрать в участок)
examples: They ran him in for the third time that year.
The sergeant threatened to run the whole group in.
He got run in for something that would not even be a ticket now.

senses.head: Break in a new engine
body: British; the American term is break in. (обкатать (двигатель))
examples: Run the engine in gently for the first thousand miles.
The manual says to run it in before towing anything.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a run-in moves it forward, RUN-in
entries.separable: yes — run in the suspect or run the suspect in, and a pronoun must separate the pair: run him in, never ✗ run in him.
entries.register: informal and dated in the arrest sense; the engine sense is British
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses — hauling somebody to the station, and the British run the engine in gently over the first thousand miles.
entries.passive: yes, and the entry's own example is a passive: he got run in for something that would not even be a ticket now, the engine should be run in gently before you tow anything.
entries.see also: run into, run down, run out

entries.meaning: To meet somebody by chance, to collide with something, to hit a problem, or to reach a large figure.
examples: I ran into my old roommate at the airport.
She runs into him at the same coffee shop twice a week.
The truck ran into a guardrail in the fog.
He ran into the doorframe in the dark.
We have run into the same problem every quarter.
If you run into trouble, call the desk.
Repairs could run into six figures.

senses.head: Meet by chance
body: The most common sense by far, and always accidental. (случайно встретить, натолкнуться на)
examples: I ran into my old roommate at the airport.
She runs into him at the same coffee shop twice a week.

senses.head: Collide with
body: With a vehicle or on foot. (врезаться в, наехать на)
examples: The truck ran into a guardrail in the fog.
He ran into the doorframe in the dark.

senses.head: Hit a problem
body: Trouble, delays, resistance, a bug. (столкнуться с, наткнуться на (проблему))
examples: We have run into the same problem every quarter.
If you run into trouble, call the desk.

senses.head: Reach a figure
body: Of costs and casualties: run into the millions. (достигать, доходить до (суммы))
examples: Repairs could run into six figures.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb; into reduces to /ˈɪntə/
entries.русский: случайно встретить; врезаться в; столкнуться с (проблемой); достигать (суммы)
entries.separable: no — into never lets go of its object: ran into my old roommate, ran into her. ✗ ran my old roommate into, ✗ ran her into. Compare run in, which is a true particle and does separate: ran him in. One letter of difference, opposite behavior.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after into
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 to 3, but accidental, so the progressive marks habit rather than an event in progress: she runs into him at the same coffee shop twice a week. Sense 4 (repairs could run into six figures) is stative — a measurement, not an act: ✗ repairs are running into six figures.
entries.passive: no in the chance-meeting and problem senses — ✗ my old roommate was run into at the airport, ✗ the same problem has been run into every quarter. The collision sense is marginal at best: ?the guardrail was run into by a truck in the fog.
entries.see also: run across, run in, run up against, meet up with

entries.meaning: To leave suddenly, to print copies, to drive somebody away, or, of water, to drain off a surface.
examples: He ran off before the check came.
She ran off to Reno and got married on a Tuesday.
Can you run off thirty of these before the meeting?
I ran a few extra off in case.
Run them off double-sided.
The rancher ran them off his land twice.
The rain runs off the clay instead of soaking in.

senses.head: Leave suddenly, elope
body: Intransitive, often with with somebody or to somewhere. (удрать, сбежать)
examples: He ran off before the check came.
She ran off to Reno and got married on a Tuesday.

senses.head: Print or copy
body: From the old duplicating machines; the object is the copies. (отпечатать, размножить (копии))
examples: Can you run off thirty of these before the meeting?
I ran a few extra off in case.
Run them off double-sided.

senses.head: Drive somebody away
body: With the person as the object, often run them off the property. (прогнать, выгнать)
examples: The rancher ran them off his land twice.

senses.head: Drain away
body: Of rain and meltwater; the noun runoff is the water itself, or a second election. (стекать, сбегать (о воде))
examples: The rain runs off the clay instead of soaking in.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun a runoff moves it forward, RUN-off
entries.separable: yes in the transitive senses — run off fifty copies or run fifty copies off, and a pronoun must go in the middle: run them off, never ✗ run off them. Senses 1 and 4 take no object at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense — fleeing (1), copying (2), driving somebody away (3), and water draining (4). Sense 4 takes an inanimate subject: the rain runs off the clay.
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses 2 and 3: thirty copies were run off before the meeting, they were run off his land twice. No in senses 1 and 4, which have no object: ✗ Reno was run off to, ✗ the clay is run off by the rain.
entries.see also: run off with, run away, make off

entries.meaning: To leave with somebody you should not have, or with something that was not yours.
examples: He ran off with his brother's girlfriend and moved to Tampa.
The treasurer ran off with eleven thousand dollars.
Somebody ran off with the good scissors again.
She left it on the bench for a minute and a kid ran off with it.
Two of the horses had run off with their blankets still on.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the object follows the whole phrase: ran off with the money, ran off with it. ✗ ran the money off with, ✗ ran it off with.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in both senses — eloping with a person and making off with a thing. Punctual, so the past is its home tense: the treasurer ran off with eleven thousand dollars.
entries.passive: no — like the other three-part verbs of taking, it will not promote its object: ✗ eleven thousand dollars was run off with by the treasurer, ✗ the good scissors were run off with again.
entries.see also: run away with, make off with, run off

entries.meaning: To continue longer than expected, to talk without stopping, or to be powered by a particular fuel.
examples: The meeting ran on until almost seven.
The trial had run on for eleven weeks.
He ran on about his knee surgery for twenty minutes.
She does tend to run on once she gets going.
The generator runs on propane.
Half the fleet still runs on diesel.
That whole office runs on coffee and spite.

senses.head: Continue too long
body: Of meetings, sentences, and seasons. The grammar term run-on sentence comes from here. (затягиваться, тянуться)
examples: The meeting ran on until almost seven.
The trial had run on for eleven weeks.

senses.head: Talk without stopping
body: Often run on about something. (тараторить, болтать без умолку)
examples: He ran on about his knee surgery for twenty minutes.
She does tend to run on once she gets going.

senses.head: Be powered by
body: With the fuel or the power source after on. (работать на (топливе, энергии))
examples: The generator runs on propane.
Half the fleet still runs on diesel.
That whole office runs on coffee and spite.

entries.pronunciation note: when it means "go on too long" the particle takes the stress; in runs on diesel it is a preposition and the stress stays on the verb, RUN-on
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle) in senses 1 and 2; prepositional verb in sense 3
entries.separable: nothing to separate — in every sense the verb takes no object of its own. In sense 3 the fuel follows on and never moves: runs on propane, runs on it.
entries.transitive: no; sense 3 takes an object after the preposition on
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1 and 2 (a meeting running long, a person talking on), both naturally progressive: the trial had been running on for eleven weeks. Sense 3, run on propane, is stative — a permanent property of the machine: ✗ the generator is running on propane means it is doing so right now, not what it is built for.
entries.passive: no — objectless in senses 1 and 2, and the fuel will not move to subject in sense 3: ✗ propane is run on by the generator, ✗ diesel is still run on by half the fleet.
entries.see also: ride on, run over, run out

entries.meaning: Of a supply or a period of time, to come to an end.
examples: The milk ran out before breakfast.
Batteries run out fast in the cold.
Our patience had run out long before the third apology.
Her lease runs out in June.
The clock ran out with the ball still in the air.
His visa had run out two weeks earlier.

senses.head: Be used up
body: Of milk, gas, patience, money. (кончаться, иссякать)
examples: The milk ran out before breakfast.
Batteries run out fast in the cold.
Our patience had run out long before the third apology.

senses.head: Expire
body: Of a lease, a warranty, a passport, or the clock. (истекать, заканчиваться (о сроке))
examples: Her lease runs out in June.
The clock ran out with the ball still in the air.
His visa had run out two weeks earlier.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress
entries.separable: nothing to separate — here the supply is the subject, not an object: the milk ran out. When you want the person as the subject, the verb picks up a preposition: run out of.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — a change of state, with the supply or the period as subject: the milk ran out before breakfast, her lease runs out in June. The progressive means approaching the end: we're running out.
entries.passive: no — intransitive, and the supply is already the subject: ✗ the milk was run out, ✗ her lease was run out in June. For a personal subject the verb has to add a preposition: we ran out of milk.
entries.see also: run out of, run out on, pay up

entries.meaning: To use up your supply of something.
examples: We ran out of milk before breakfast.
He had run out of excuses by the third week.
The store runs out of ice every Fourth of July.
I ran out of gas two exits from home.
She never runs out of things to say.
If we run out of chairs, people can stand.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle; of reduces to /əv/
entries.separable: no — what you have used up follows the whole phrase: ran out of gas, ran out of it. ✗ ran gas out of, ✗ ran it out of.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — a change of state reached at a point in time: I ran out of gas two exits from home. The progressive means nearly: we're running out of chairs.
entries.passive: no — the exhausted supply cannot become the subject: ✗ gas was run out of two exits from home, ✗ excuses had been run out of by the third week.
entries.see also: run out, run up, pay off

entries.meaning: To abandon somebody who was counting on you.
examples: He ran out on his family in 1989 and never wrote.
Two investors ran out on the deal a week before closing.
Don't run out on me now.
She has never run out on anybody in her life.
The drummer ran out on them halfway through the tour.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on the middle particle
entries.separable: no — the person you abandoned follows the whole phrase: ran out on his family, ran out on them. ✗ ran his family out on, ✗ ran them out on.
entries.transitive: yes, and the object is a person or an obligation
entries.register: everyday — reproachful; it is an accusation, not a neutral description
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — abandoning somebody at a moment: he ran out on his family in 1989. Reproachful, so it is nearly always a past-tense accusation.
entries.passive: restricted — it occurs but reads stiffly: ?she was run out on by the only investor she trusted. Americans say she was walked out on or, better, keep it active: he ran out on her.
entries.see also: quit on, run away, run off

entries.meaning: To hit something with a vehicle, to go past a time limit, to review something quickly, or to overflow.
examples: A car ran over the mailbox during the storm.
He ran the hose over with the mower.
She braked hard so she wouldn't run it over.
The meeting ran over by twenty minutes.
Every panel he chairs runs over.
Let's run over the agenda one more time.
She ran over it twice on the way in.
The sink ran over while she was on the phone.

senses.head: Hit with a vehicle
body: The car passes over the thing; compare run down, where it knocks the thing forward. (переехать, задавить)
examples: A car ran over the mailbox during the storm.
He ran the hose over with the mower.
She braked hard so she wouldn't run it over.

senses.head: Go past a time limit
body: Intransitive, of meetings and shows. (затянуться, выйти за рамки времени)
examples: The meeting ran over by twenty minutes.
Every panel he chairs runs over.

senses.head: Review quickly
body: Prepositional, and inseparable: the notes, the agenda, the plan. (бегло просмотреть, пройтись по)
examples: Let's run over the agenda one more time.
She ran over it twice on the way in.

senses.head: Overflow
body: Of a tub, a gutter, or a cup. (перелиться через край)
examples: The sink ran over while she was on the phone.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress in senses 1 and 2; in the "review" sense it is a preposition and the stress stays on the verb, RUN-oh-vur
entries.русский: переехать (машиной); затянуться; бегло просмотреть; перелиться через край
entries.type: phrasal verb (verb + particle) in sense 1; prepositional verb in sense 3
entries.separable: it depends on the sense, and the difference is worth memorizing. Hitting something with a car is a particle and separates: ran over the cat, ran the cat over, ran it over. Reviewing something is a preposition and does not: run over the agenda, run over it, and ✗ run the agenda over — which, if anyone said it, would mean you drove across the paper.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all four senses: hitting something with a car (1), going past a time limit (2), reviewing quickly (3), and overflowing (4). Senses 2 and 4 take the situation or the container as subject: the meeting ran over, the sink ran over.
entries.passive: yes in sense 1, where it is the ordinary way to say it: the mailbox was run over during the storm, the dog got run over on Route 9. No in senses 2 and 4, which have no object: ✗ twenty minutes were run over. Sense 3 passivizes only awkwardly: ?the agenda was run over one more time.
entries.see also: run down, run through, read over

entries.meaning: To go over something from start to finish, to spend money fast, or, of a theme, to be present all the way along.
examples: Let's run through it once before they get here.
The crew ran through the safety checks twice.
She runs through her opening in the car every morning.
He ran through the whole advance in four months.
They had run through two boxes of paper by noon.
A streak of stubbornness runs through that entire family.
He was run through in the second act and died beautifully.

senses.head: Rehearse, go over
body: Lines, a routine, a checklist, a plan. The noun a run-through is the rehearsal itself. (прогнать, отрепетировать, пройтись по)
examples: Let's run through it once before they get here.
The crew ran through the safety checks twice.
She runs through her opening in the car every morning.

senses.head: Spend or use up quickly
body: Money, savings, an inheritance, a box of tissues. (промотать, быстро израсходовать)
examples: He ran through the whole advance in four months.
They had run through two boxes of paper by noon.

senses.head: Be present throughout
body: Of a theme, a vein, a streak. (проходить через, пронизывать)
examples: A streak of stubbornness runs through that entire family.

senses.head: Pierce with a blade
body: Archaic, and now only in historical writing. (проткнуть, пронзить)
examples: He was run through in the second act and died beautifully.

entries.pronunciation note: a preposition here, so the stress stays on the verb; the noun a run-through moves it forward and is stressed RUN-throo as well
entries.русский: прогнать, отрепетировать; бегло просмотреть; промотать (деньги); пронизывать
entries.separable: no — through keeps its object, and the pronoun proves it: run through it, never ✗ run it through in this meaning. (✗ run the list through is wrong; run through the list is right.)
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after through
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in senses 1, 2, and 4 — rehearsing, spending fast, and the archaic piercing with a blade. Sense 3, a streak of stubbornness runs through that family, is stative: it describes a standing property, not an event, and rejects the progressive (✗ is running through that family).
entries.passive: yes in senses 1 and 4, and the entry's own example is one: he was run through in the second act, the safety checks were run through twice. Sense 2 is acceptable but stiff (?the whole advance was run through in four months), and sense 3 has no passive: ✗ that family is run through by a streak of stubbornness.
entries.see also: run over, read through, run by

entries.meaning: To accumulate a large amount of something owed, to hoist something, or to sew something quickly.
examples: He ran up a four-hundred-dollar tab.
They ran enormous legal bills up fighting the permit.
She ran it up on a card she was supposed to have cut in half.
They run the flag up at seven every morning.
Her grandmother could run up a dress in an afternoon.
Prices climb in the run-up to the holidays.

senses.head: Accumulate charges or debt
body: Bills, tabs, legal fees, mileage. (накопить, набрать (счета, долги))
examples: He ran up a four-hundred-dollar tab.
They ran enormous legal bills up fighting the permit.
She ran it up on a card she was supposed to have cut in half.

senses.head: Hoist
body: A flag, a sail. (поднять (флаг, парус))
examples: They run the flag up at seven every morning.

senses.head: Sew quickly
body: Slightly dated, and more common in British English. (быстро сшить, смастерить)
examples: Her grandmother could run up a dress in an afternoon.

senses.head: Run up to — the approach to an event
body: In the noun the run-up to an election or a holiday. (преддверие, период перед)
examples: Prices climb in the run-up to the holidays.

entries.pronunciation note: the particle carries the stress; the noun the run-up moves it forward, RUN-up
entries.separable: yes — run up a bill or run a bill up, and a pronoun must go in the middle: run it up, never ✗ run up it. Compare run up against, which never separates at all.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all three senses — piling up charges, hoisting a flag, and sewing something quickly. Sense 1 is gradual and takes the progressive well: he was running up a tab all night.
entries.passive: yes, and idiomatic in every transitive sense: a four-hundred-dollar tab was run up in one evening, the flag is run up at seven every morning, the whole dress was run up in an afternoon.
entries.see also: run up against, pay down, ring up

entries.meaning: To meet an obstacle you cannot simply go around.
examples: The project ran up against the zoning board in its first month.
She ran up against the same objection at every meeting.
We ran up against a wall of paperwork.
Anybody who tries this runs up against the same math.
They had run up against it before and knew what was coming.
entries.pronunciation note: the last particle carries the stress
entries.separable: no — the obstacle follows the whole phrase: ran up against the zoning board, ran up against it. ✗ ran the zoning board up against. Contrast run up, which separates freely: ran a bill up.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — meeting an obstacle at a point in time, with the project or the person as subject: the project ran up against the zoning board in its first month.
entries.passive: no — the obstacle stays where it is: ✗ the zoning board was run up against by the project, ✗ the same objection was run up against at every meeting.
entries.see also: run into, run up, run across

entries.meaning: To take an idea and develop it on your own without waiting for more instruction.
examples: It's a rough draft — take it and run with it.
She ran with the suggestion and had a prototype by Friday.
They gave him one sentence of direction and he ran with it.
Somebody in marketing ran with the joke and put it on a billboard.
We can run with the cheaper version if the budget stays flat.
entries.pronunciation note: a preposition, so the stress stays on the verb
entries.русский: взяться за, развить (идею) и довести до конца
entries.separable: no — with keeps its object: run with the idea, run with it. ✗ run the idea with.
entries.transitive: yes, always takes an object after with
entries.register: informal — American workplace speech, usually approving
entries.verb type: action — dynamic — taking an idea and developing it, usually over a stretch of time: she was running with the suggestion before anyone approved it.
entries.passive: no — the idea cannot be promoted: ✗ the suggestion was run with by her, ✗ the joke was run with by somebody in marketing. Keep it active, or say the suggestion was taken up.
entries.see also: run by, rise to, put forward
